messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame was seven years old the first time his father’s belt landed across his back, the rough leather stitching imprinted into his skin like a brand. It happened in the basement of their house, where the concrete floor stayed cold even in summer, and where his father’s heavy footsteps on the stairs always preceded the inevitable. The buckle, the chill, the rhythm of those approaching steps—those three sensations became the coordinates of his childhood terror. By the time he left home at eighteen, Kwame had learned to read those cues with a precision that felt more like survival than memory.

Now at twenty-seven, driving his Uber through the streets of Chicago, those same cues still hijack his nervous system without warning. A passenger slides into the back seat wearing a thick wool coat, and the texture under Kwame’s fingers as he adjusts the headrest sends a jolt through his chest. Immediately his shoulders tighten, his eyes dart to the rearview mirror, and his foot hovers over the accelerator—he is on high alert, scanning for danger even when the passenger is just a tired commuter. In those moments, the safety others take for granted feels like a lie; no matter how calm the street looks, his body is already braced for the blow. To quiet that alarm, he reaches for the vape pen tucked in his console, taking a quick draw of marijuana that dulls the edges of the panic, or he cranks the volume on a podcast until the footsteps in his memory are drowned out. But the vape pen itself has become its own trigger: its cool plastic against his lips, the faint smell of the vapor, the act of taking a sharp inhale in the dark—each of these now pulls him back without warning to the cold concrete floor and the belt, as if the strategy he uses to escape has woven itself into the texture of the memory.

Kwame has come to believe that something inside him has permanently split. His body keeps reacting as though the basement is right there, as though his father could walk into the cab at any moment, and that betrayal—the way his own skin refuses to believe he is safe—has convinced him he is broken beyond repair. He no longer attends the church where he once served as an usher; the warmth of that community now feels like a foreign language he can no longer speak. Intimacy of any kind terrifies him, not because he doesn't want it, but because being close to someone would mean letting down the defenses he has built. Instead, he pours himself into the cab, sometimes accepting late-night rides into unfamiliar neighborhoods, driving at speeds that make his passengers grip the door handles. The risk feels like the only time his body matches his internal state—when the threat is real, at least his hypervigilance makes sense. But the constant watchfulness also sharpens his perception of every texture and temperature, until even the cool air from the AC on his arm can drag him back to that basement floor.

His strategies for coping have only deepened the hole. Distracting himself with loud music or streaming videos while he waits for a fare keeps the memories at bay, but it also means he often misses the warning cues—a pedestrian’s footsteps too close, the scrape of a coat against the seat—until they are suddenly right on top of him, and the startle response leaves him shaking for blocks. The marijuana, which he uses almost daily, leaves him feeling foggy and isolated, reinforcing the idea that he has lost his connection to the world and to his own community. He lives alone, his only regular conversation the brief exchanges with passengers he will never see again. Last week, after a fare touched his arm to thank him, the particular coolness of the hand—rough and dry—sent him into a panic that forced him to pull over and hyperventilate for ten minutes in a gas station parking lot. It was the first time he admitted to himself that he could not keep running this way. He scheduled an appointment with a therapist, his hands trembling as he typed the intake form, because what he fears most now is not the abuse itself, but the certainty that he has already become someone who cannot be helped.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals (e.g., belief of being broken) drive or amplify the sense of threat; instead, the threat (body reacting as if in danger) is shown to cause negative appraisals.
